title: VH-GPO: Verified Handoff forLLM Agent Reinforcement Learning

paper.title: VH-GPO: Verified Handoff for LLM Agent Reinforcement Learning
paper.abstract:
Abstract Reinforcement learning (RL) plays a key role in training large language models
(LLMs) to solve complex tasks through outcome-based feedback.
Group-relative RL methods such as GRPO train
language-model agents by comparing the outcomes of multiple rollouts for the
same task. This mechanism is effective when outcomes vary, but if every
trajectory in a group fails with the same reward, relative advantages collapse
toward zero and the group supplies no useful learning signal. When the
trainable agent’s rollouts fail to produce any successful trajectory, one
possible solution is to introduce a frozen teacher policy. We refer to the
trainable agent as the student. The teacher attempts recovery from a state
reached by the student, and its continuation is retained only if the
environment verifies success. Yet allowing the teacher to complete
the remaining task makes the entire recovered suffix teacher-generated,
turning supervision into off-policy imitation and weakening a key benefit of
RL: learning on the state distribution induced by the student. We therefore
ask: after a teacher has repaired a student failure, when should control return
to the student? Our core insight is that the teacher should act only long
enough to cross what the student cannot yet handle, then hand back control so
that successful experience is again student-generated. We formalize this idea
as outcome-verified teacher–student handoff and instantiate it in
Verified Handoff for Group Policy Optimization (VH-GPO). Given a verified
teacher recovery, VH-GPO returns control to the student at the earliest
independently confirmed handoff point found within a bounded search budget.
With Qwen2.5-1.5B,
VH-GPO increases success rates over GRPO from 59.38% to 94.79% on ALFWorld
and from 71.62% to 77.34% on WebShop. Improvements also hold with the 7B
student, for which additional teacher and student output tokens amount to
1.77% and 2.61% of regular student rollout output tokens on ALFWorld and
WebShop, respectively. Ablation studies validate the design of
VH-GPO and demonstrate the effectiveness of its key components.
The teacher need not solve every problem for the student; instead, it should
provide just enough support when the student struggles to help it find a way
forward and gradually learn to solve problems independently.

Group-relative RL methods such as GRPO train language-model agents by comparing the outcomes of multiple rollouts for the same task. This mechanism is effective when outcomes vary, but if every trajectory in a group fails with the same reward, relative advantages collapse toward zero and the group supplies no useful learning signal. When the trainable agent’s rollouts fail to produce any successful trajectory, one possible solution is to introduce a frozen teacher policy. We refer to the trainable agent as the student. The teacher attempts recovery from a state reached by the student, and its continuation is retained only if the environment verifies success. Yet allowing the teacher to complete the remaining task makes the entire recovered suffix teacher-generated, turning supervision into off-policy imitation and weakening a key benefit of RL: learning on the state distribution induced by the student. We therefore ask: after a teacher has repaired a student failure, when should control return to the student? Our core insight is that the teacher should act only long enough to cross what the student cannot yet handle, then hand back control so that successful experience is again student-generated. We formalize this idea as outcome-verified teacher–student handoff and instantiate it in Verified Handoff for Group Policy Optimization (VH-GPO). Given a verified teacher recovery, VH-GPO returns control to the student at the earliest independently confirmed handoff point found within a bounded search budget. With Qwen2.5-1.5B, VH-GPO increases success rates over GRPO from 59.38% to 94.79% on ALFWorld and from 71.62% to 77.34% on WebShop. Improvements also hold with the 7B student, for which additional teacher and student output tokens amount to 1.77% and 2.61% of regular student rollout output tokens on ALFWorld and WebShop, respectively. Ablation studies validate the design of VH-GPO and demonstrate the effectiveness of its key components. The teacher need not solve every problem for the student; instead, it should provide just enough support when the student struggles to help it find a way forward and gradually learn to solve problems independently. 1 1 footnotetext: Beihang University. Email: zp@luxitech.cn . 1 Introduction Reinforcement learning (RL) has become an important component of large language model (LLM) post-training, improving instruction following and reasoning ( Ouyang et al., 2022 ; Guo et al., 2025 ) . Beyond text generation, LLM agents reason over observations and issue actions to external environments, including web browsing ( Nakano et al., 2022 ; Yao et al., 2023 ) . RL is particularly attractive for improving such agents because the agent learns from trajectories sampled by its own evolving policy. The resulting supervision reflects the states, actions, and errors that the policy will actually encounter, rather than only those chosen by a fixed demonstrator. In long-horizon environments, however, outcome supervision is often extremely sparse: an agent may execute many locally plausible actions and still receive no terminal reward. This problem is especially acute for tasks that require several dependent subgoals, such as manipulating multiple objects in ALFWorld ( Shridhar et al., 2021 ) or satisfying multiple product constraints in WebShop ( Yao et al., 2022 ) . Group-relative policy optimization methods such as GRPO ( Shao et al., 2024 ) learn by comparing the outcomes of multiple rollouts for the same task. When every rollout fails with the same terminal reward, however, the group-relative advantages collapse to zero, leaving no outcome-based policy-gradient signal to guide improvement on that task. Such groups expose failures of the current policy without providing a successful alternative to learn from. If these failures recur, the corresponding capability gaps can persist even as the policy improves on tasks with informative reward contrast. DAPO maintains informative training batches by filtering out all-success and all-failure groups through dynamic sampling ( Yu et al., 2025 ) . When zero-advantage groups are frequent, as can occur early in training on sparse-reward tasks, dynamic sampling requires additional rollouts to replace discarded groups and fill each training batch, increasing rollout cost. Yet filtering alone does not provide corrective targets for the discarded failures. Fine-grained grouping and graph-based credit assignment improve attribution within sampled experience ( Feng et al., 2025 ; Cheng et al., 2026 ) , yet cannot supply a successful continuation when none is present. This motivates a mechanism that turns selected zero-signal failures into verified learning opportunities. When the current policy cannot produce a successful continuation, a natural recovery mechanism is to invoke a frozen auxiliary policy from a failure state that the policy has already reached. The continuation is retained only if the environment verifies terminal success ( Xia et al., 2026a ) , thereby turning an otherwise uninformative failure into a grounded positive target. From this point onward, we call the trainable policy the student and the frozen recovery policy the teacher . A full teacher continuation can convert a failed trajectory into a verified success. However, the longer the teacher remains in control, the more student-generated RL experience is replaced by off-policy imitation on the teacher’s state–action distribution. This raises the question of when a recovering teacher should return control to the student. We formulate outcome-verified teacher–student handoff as a training principle: the teacher corrects a student failure, then hands back control once independent student continuations verify successful completion. Based on this principle, we propose Verified Handoff for Group Policy Optimization (VH-GPO). For an all-failure, zero-signal group, VH-GPO invokes a frozen teacher from a student-reached state and retains its recovery only if the environment verifies success. It then tests states along that recovery to identify, within a bounded search budget, the earliest tested state from which student success is independently confirmed. The resulting short teacher bridge and verified student continuation provide three auxiliary training signals: state-aligned action preferences, teacher-bridge supervision, and student-resume supervision. These signals complement the unchanged root GRPO update. The teacher is used only during training; the student acts independently at inference time. Experiments on ALFWorld and WebShop with Qwen2.5-Instruct students at 1.5B and 7B scales show that VH-GPO consistently improves the corresponding GRPO baseline. With the 1.5B student, success increases from 59.38 % 59.38\% to 94.79 % 94.79\% on ALFWorld and from 71.62 % 71.62\% to 77.34 % 77.34\% on WebShop. With the 7B student, success increases from 78.12 % 78.12\% to 95.57 % 95.57\% on ALFWorld and from 71.61 % 71.61\% to 79.69 % 79.69\% on WebShop. These gains require little additional generation: in the 7B runs, all additional teacher and student generation totals just 1.77 % 1.77\% of the tokens generated by regular student rollouts on ALFWorld and 2.61 % 2.61\% on WebShop. Our contributions are threefold: • We highlight the lack of corrective learning targets in all-failure, zero-signal groups and formulate outcome-verified teacher–student handoff as a training principle: the teacher should provide only the support needed to restore the student’s ability to complete the task, then return control once independent completion is verified. • We introduce VH-GPO, which implements this principle through outcome-verified teacher recovery and bounded search for the earliest tested, independently confirmed student handoff. The resulting relays supply state-aligned action preferences, teacher-bridge supervision, and student-resume supervision alongside the unchanged root GRPO objective. • Experiments on ALFWorld and WebShop show that VH-GPO improves overall task success over GRPO and competitive group-based RL baselines at both 1.5B and 7B scales, with modest generation overhead: additional teacher and student generation totals only 1.77 % 1.77\% and 2.61 % 2.61\% of root rollout output tokens on the two benchmarks, respectively, in the 7B runs. 2 Related Work Reinforcement learning for language-model agents. RL trains language-model agents for web interaction, device control, and search ( Qi et al., 2025 ; Bai et al., 2024 ; Jin et al., 2025 ) , supported by environment and training frameworks such as AgentGym, AgentGym-RL, and Agent Lightning ( Xi et al., 2025 ; Xi et al., 2026 ; Luo et al., 2025 ) . PPO and ArCHer provide actor–critic approaches to sequential decision-making ( Schulman et al., 2017 ; Zhou et al., 2024 ) , while RAGEN examines multi-turn training instabilities, including reward-variance collapse ( Wang et al., 2025 ) . Critic-free methods include REINFORCE leave-one-out and GRPO ( Ahmadian et al., 2024 ; Shao et al., 2024 ) ; REINFORCE++, Dr. GRPO, and GSPO refine normalization or importance weighting ( Hu et al., 2025 ; Liu et al., 2025 ; Zheng et al., 2025 ) . Group-relative estimation depends on within-task reward variation. DAPO filters out all-success and all-failure groups through dynamic sampling ( Yu et al., 2025 ) . Fine-grained credit assignment for multi-turn agents. Process supervision supplies intermediate feedback through human or automatically generated step labels ( Lightman et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2024 ) . MCTS-based preference learning, ReST-MCTS*, and Agent Q use search to construct finer-grained training signals ( Xie et al., 2024 ; Zhang et al., 2024 ; Putta et al., 2024 ) . VinePPO estimates advantages using Monte Carlo continuations from intermediate states ( Kazemnejad et al., 2025 ) ; VH-GPO uses such continuations to verify student resumability. For interactive agents, GiGPO combines episode-level advantages with same-state action groups ( Feng et al., 2025 ) , HGPO groups steps by shared historical context ( He et al., 2026 ) , and GraphGPO assigns credit through a state-transition graph and distance to a verified goal ( Cheng et al., 2026 ) . Distillation for LLM agents. STaR, ReST, ReST EM , RAFT, and ReST meets ReAct learn from successful or feedback-selected model outputs ( Zelikman et al., 2022 ; Gulcehre et al., 2023 ; Singh et al., 2024 ; Dong et al., 2023 ; Aksitov et al., 2023 ) , while self-imitation learning reinforces past good decisions through an off-policy actor–critic objective ( Oh et al., 2018 ) . Teacher supervision can supply additional targets, including rationales in Distilling Step-by-Step ( Hsieh et al., 2023 ) . Generalized Knowledge Distillation and MiniLLM reduce distribution mismatch using student-generated sequences and teacher feedback ( Agarwal et al., 2024 ; Gu et al., 2024 ) , but matching teacher predictions alone does not verify environment success. Outcome-Verified Comparative Self-Distillation (OVCSD) ( Xia et al., 2026a ) organizes failed student rollouts into a prefix tree, invokes a teacher from selected student states, and retains successful continuations for divergence-level comparison and suffix distillation.
